# Mobile changes the edges {#sec-mobile}

Qt Quick lets a shared application core reach Android and iOS. The device changes the view,
lifecycle, and permissions, not the reason to keep state separate.

## Touch and lifecycle shape the view {#sec-mobile-device}

Design for fingers, smaller rotating screens, and suspension at any time. Save after meaningful
edits, not only when the app quits. Use `QStandardPaths` because each app has its own
sandbox.

Touch targets need enough room for a finger, and hover cannot be the only way to discover an
action. Orientation and screen density can change the space available to a view. The operating
system can suspend or terminate an app while it is in the background, so do not rely on a
normal quit to save work. Keeping these concerns in the view and platform boundary helps the
core remain shared with the desktop app.

## Native toolchains build the package {#sec-mobile-build}

Android needs its SDK and NDK; iOS needs Xcode and an Apple toolchain. Install the matching Qt
kits, then let CMake configure against the target platform.

Qt provides separate kits for Android and iOS. A mobile build is cross-compiled with the
platform toolchain; test on the target device as well as an emulator or simulator, because
input, graphics, and lifecycle behaviour can differ.

## Permissions ask at the moment of need {#sec-permissions}

Declare a permission in platform metadata and request it when a feature needs it. Explain the
benefit in the UI. A request for camera access makes sense beside scanning, not at first launch.
Android uses its manifest; iOS uses `Info.plist` with a usage description. Qt provides a
common API for requesting supported permissions at runtime.

::: {.more}
**Read more:** [Qt mobile development](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/mobiledevelopment.html) and
[Qt permissions](https://doc.qt.io/qt-6/permissions.html).
:::
